title: Not the whole life at once
hookLine: don't let the picture of your whole life crush you; take this piece (Meditations 8.36)

lines: THE WHOLE YEAR ON YOUR CHEST.
NOT THE WHOLE LIFE AT ONCE.
cards: It's Sunday night and you open the calendar. Not this week: the whole year. The lease renewal, the move, the parent who's getting older, the money that has to stretch until spring.
In thirty seconds every trouble you might ever have is sitting on your chest at once. None of it is happening yet. All of it feels heavy.
Marcus Aurelius ruled through years of war and plague, and a few entries after yesterday's, he wrote himself a short note about exactly this feeling.

teach.b: In book eight Marcus tells himself not to let his thoughts gather up, all at once, every hardship he expects to meet.
George Long's 1862 translation begins it plainly: “Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life.”
Instead, with each thing as it arrives, ask: what in this is actually unbearable, past bearing? He thinks you'd be embarrassed to answer.
Most present moments, looked at alone, are smaller than the dread that came with them. Then a shrinking trick. Neither the past nor the future weighs on you, he writes, only the present.

teach.h: MARK THE PRESENT OFF BY ITSELF.
teach.b: And even the present gets smaller if you mark it off by itself, draw its edges tight around this hour, and ask your mind whether it really can't hold out against something so little. This isn't avoidance.
Marcus planned campaigns and wrote laws; he didn't stop thinking ahead.

teach.h: PLAN THE YEAR, CARRY THE DAY.
teach.b: The note is about carrying, not planning: you can plan the year on paper and still carry only today.
And the week, looking back: not by reputation, steadily, no blaming, fig, what it means, one action at a time, and now, this piece only.
Book eight keeps shrinking the field until what's left is something a person can actually do.

how: Many people who read the Meditations keep a list for today rather than a worry list for the year, and when dread about the future rises they ask Marcus's question of the present hour: what here is actually unbearable?

games.q: not the whole life at once — tap the pairs.
p: what Marcus says not to picture at once
smaller when marked off by itself

s: Marcus advises picturing every future trouble so you're ready for it
he tells himself not to gather all expected troubles at once, but to ask about each one as it comes.
Marcus says only the present weighs on us
neither past nor future, he writes, only the present, and it shrinks when you mark it off by itself.
the note means Marcus stopped planning ahead
he ran campaigns and wrote laws; the note is about what you carry, not whether you plan.

games.q: it's sunday night and the whole year is on your chest. you're Marcus with his notebook. what do you write?
o: list every trouble ahead so none surprises you.
take this piece, and ask what in it is truly unbearable.
decide not to think about anything at all.
games.why: he tells himself not to picture the whole of life at once, and to ask of each present thing what in it is past bearing. he expects the honest answer to be: very little.

practice: Let the big picture come up for a moment, the year, the list, the worries, and notice its weight. Now draw a small box around today and name two or three things that actually have to happen before sleep, no more.
Set everything outside the box on a shelf; tomorrow it gets its own box.

wordCard.voice: George Long, whose 1862 translation renders Marcus's note: do not disturb yourself by thinking of the whole of your life. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the present, what is at hand. Marcus wrote the Meditations in Greek.

carryVoice: Your line: this piece only. The present, marked off, is small enough to hold. A week of book eight, done.

sources.q: Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life.
